title: EDUCATION: The Ultimate Factorising Booklet
author: Peter Mattock
summary: Peter Mattock describes the creation of a free, AI-assisted factorising booklet built on Engelmann's Direct Instruction principles and Boulton's Unstoppable Learning approach. The core philosophy is that every child can learn mathematics if taught correctly, and that failure to learn reflects flawed instruction or curriculum sequencing, never the child. The booklet sequences learning from division of algebraic terms by constants through dividing linear terms, two-term division, taking a single term outside the bracket (the 'plutonium atom'), finding the highest common factor, and fully factorising expressions. The sequencing is deliberate: each step automates prerequisite skills so the final factorisation routine feels inevitable rather than arbitrary. Mattock used Dr. Dario Emanuele's AI lesson-creation tool and responded to community feedback by adding the HCF section. The booklet is available as a free download.
points: Engelmann/Boulton principle: if a student does not learn, the instruction or sequencing is at fault -- never the child.
The 'plutonium atom': taking any term outside a bracket (undone by division inside) is a powerful, generalisable mathematical transformation.
Deliberate prerequisite sequencing: division of terms, two-term division, HCF, full factorisation -- each step prepares the next.
AI lesson-creation tools enable well-sequenced free resource production that previously required significant expertise and time.
Community feedback improved the booklet -- specifically by adding the HCF section recommended by substack readers.
quotes: Their approach has at its heart the fundamental belief that every child can learn maths if taught correctly.
This approach says that if the student does not learn the instruction or sequencing of curriculum is at fault, not the child, never the child!
The beauty lies in knowing one can take anything out of the bracket, not just a factor, so long as you then undo your multiplication with a division inside.
The goal is that, once we get to the prompt 'Fully factorise' students are well rehearsed in all the component pieces that the routine makes total sense to them and they can apply it flexibly.
Another shout out here goes to the substack community who helped me with this and convinced me to put in the highest common factor section, which is much needed!
